nature-acct-089.title: Environmental accounting: keeping the books on nature
nature-acct-089.text: By 2007, a United Nations assessment found, 49 countries were using environmental-economic accounting. Environmental accounting is the branch of accounting that measures, analyses and reports money and non-money information about environmental impacts. For a company it judges environmental performance and informs people inside and outside the firm. For a nation or region it records how the economy affects the environment. It tracks resource use and environmental costs, such as cleaning up contaminated sites, fines and taxes, pollution-prevention technology and waste handling. A full system has two halves. Environmentally differentiated accounting measures nature's effects on the firm, in money. Ecological accounting measures the firm's effects on nature, in physical units. The field divides into global, national and corporate environmental accounting. At national level it is formalised internationally through SEEA, which builds on the System of National Accounts ({{ref:nature-econ-596}}). Why do organisations do it? Explanations range from the interests of managers and shareholders to legitimacy, stakeholder pressure and a sense of duty to account for their impacts.

nature-acct-105.title: Assets: what a business owns or controls
nature-acct-105.text: A leased building counts as a company's asset; its employees do not. In financial accounting an asset is any resource a business or other economic entity owns or controls, and control is enough: ownership is not required. More broadly, an asset is anything, physical or not, that can be used to produce economic value. A firm's balance sheet records the money value of its assets. It follows the accounting equation: assets equal liabilities, what the firm owes, plus equity, the owners' stake. Tangible assets include current assets such as cash and inventory, and fixed assets such as land, buildings and equipment. Intangible assets include patents and goodwill. Fixed assets other than land are written off against profits over their expected life through depreciation ({{ref:nature-econ-519}}). In economics, an asset is any form in which wealth can be held. Social scientists study how things like ecosystems are turned into assets.

nature-acct-096.title: Natural capital accounting: a balance sheet for nature
nature-acct-096.text: One US study estimated that air-pollution damage from coal-fired power generation is worth 0.8 to 5.6 times the value the industry adds. Figures like that come from natural capital accounting: calculating the total stocks and flows of natural resources and services in an ecosystem or region. The accounts can be kept in physical units or in money. They can guide government, business and consumer choices about using resources and land. Money-based indicators tend to be expressed as flows, physical ones as stocks. Approaches include broad indicator dashboards and composite indices. Others are indices of consumption beyond nature's limits ({{ref:nature-eecon-185}}), such as adjusted net saving and footprints ({{ref:nature-acct-027}}), and adjusted economic indicators such as green GDP. International support began with the 1987 report of {{ref:nature-eecon-222}} and the 1992 Rio Summit, whose action plan ({{ref:nature-gov-127}}) asked signatories to develop quantitative information on their activities. The 2012 conference {{ref:nature-hist-008}} was described as a watershed in worldwide interest. The Netherlands, France and the Philippines were early adopters of integrated environmental-economic accounts. In the US, Congress halted federal work on environmental accounting in 1994, after the first US integrated satellite accounts appeared.

nature-acct-114.title: Triple bottom line: people, planet and profit
nature-acct-114.text: In ordinary accounting the 'bottom line' is profit or loss. The triple bottom line adds two more, judging an organisation on social, environmental and economic results. Freer Spreckley first set out the framework in 1981. John Elkington says he coined the phrase in 1994 and developed it in his 1997 book Cannibals with Forks. His slogan 'people, planet, and profit' titled Shell's first sustainability report in 1997. The planet line asks firms to shrink the nature they use ({{ref:nature-acct-027}}), often tallying a product's true environmental cost from raw materials to disposal ({{ref:nature-acct-050}}). The profit line means economic value created after deducting all input costs, including capital, which differs from accounting profit. Measuring the people line is relatively new, problematic and often subjective. Since a 2007 UN and ICLEI standard, it has been the dominant approach to public-sector full cost accounting. Many disagree that it is the right way to improve social and environmental conditions. Critics say it treats the environment as a background externality and is hard to apply in practice.

nature-acct-094.title: Green accounting: bringing environmental costs into the results
nature-acct-094.text: Economist Peter Wood brought the term into common use in the 1980s. Green accounting tries to bring environmental costs into the financial results of an activity. Its backers argue that GDP ignores the environment, so policymakers need a model that includes green accounting. Its main aim is to help businesses manage trade-offs between ordinary economic goals and environmental ones. At national scale, green national accounting values environmental assets that measures of national wealth usually leave out, partly because they are hard to value. Its reach is limited. It is said to secure only {{ref:nature-eecon-217}}, a step toward {{ref:nature-eecon-218}}. Sources also disagree on whether it is sound at all. Critics say the using up of resources may already be counted in extraction industries, and that putting values on externalities can be arbitrary.

nature-acct-092.title: Full-cost accounting: costs counted as resources are used
nature-acct-092.text: A vehicle bought once and used for ten years is costed across all ten years, not in the year the cash is spent. That is the logic of environmental full-cost accounting, a cost-accounting method that gathers the possible environmental costs and benefits of each option under consideration. It traces direct costs and allocates indirect ones. It values goods even when no cash changes hands, such as equipment paid for by a state grant. It includes overheads, past costs such as buying equipment, and future ones such as closing a facility. Florida uses it to identify and report the actual costs of solid waste management. A major motive is anticipating market or regulatory problems that come from ignoring the whole outcome of a process. Prices can mislead: subsidies to energy and food keep them artificially low, hiding true costs and the externalities of fossil fuels and mechanised farming. The method is one part of {{ref:nature-acct-103}}, alongside human and social capital. Experts find both 'full' and 'true' troublesome labels, because the words are subjective.

nature-acct-099.title: Sustainability accounting: reporting beyond the balance sheet
nature-acct-099.text: In most countries, governments do not require companies to prepare and publish sustainability reports. Sustainability accounting, also called non-financial reporting, is how firms that do so tell outsiders such as investors and creditors about their social and environmental performance. It began in the 1970s, when environmental matters were part of a broad movement to account for firms' social effects ({{ref:nature-gov-073}}). By 1991–1995 environmental accounting almost completely dominated that movement. It is treated as a branch of financial accounting. Inside the firm, in management accounting, it supports decisions about the triple bottom line of people, planet and profit. Company sustainability reports and triple bottom line accounting are its best-known measures. The Global Reporting Initiative was set up to give organisations guidelines so that social and environmental reports are consistent. The Sustainability Accounting Standards Board standardises some metrics so investors can judge corporate risk.

nature-acct-103.title: True cost accounting: pricing the hidden effects
nature-acct-103.text: Some costs never show up in a price. True cost accounting measures and puts values on the hidden effects of economic activity on the environment, society and health. These are costs and benefits that appear neither in market prices nor in firms' profit and loss accounts. It is also called full cost accounting or multiple capital accounting, and it covers natural, human, social and produced capital. The approach is closely tied to externalities and traces back to the work of Pigou and Marshall in the 1920s. It is seen as an extension of cost-benefit analysis ({{ref:nature-val-001}}) that adds systems thinking about many stakeholders and capitals. A typical study uses a dozen or more indicators across environmental, health, social and economic domains. Much of its development has been in food and farming, where hidden costs can be large. Some effects are easier to capture than others. Greenhouse gas emissions are easy to include; effects on working conditions or cultural identity are harder to find.

nature-acct-111.title: Material flow accounting: weighing what an economy takes in
nature-acct-111.text: An economy, like a living thing, needs a constant flow of materials and energy through it. Material flow accounting treats the economy as a subsystem inside the environment and measures that flow, an idea called industrial or societal metabolism. It records the materials entering a national or regional economy, the changes in its stocks, and the outputs that leave as exports or as discharges to the environment. It covers all solid, liquid and gaseous materials moved by people or livestock, except bulk water and air, usually in tonnes per year. Materials fall into four groups: biomass, fossil energy carriers, metals and non-metallic minerals. It also counts non-market flows such as grazed biomass and mining waste rock, which made up 21% of global extraction in 2010. Direct material input is domestic extraction plus imports. Domestic material consumption is domestic extraction plus imports minus exports. The accounts are a satellite system to the national accounts and are used in SEEA.

nature-acct-110.title: Integrated reporting: one report for money and nature
nature-acct-110.text: From 2010 the Johannesburg Stock Exchange required listed companies to issue an integrated report or explain why not. Integrated reporting produces a periodic report on how a firm's strategy, governance, performance and prospects create value over time. It presents financial and other value-relevant information together, aimed mainly at those who allocate financial capital. Backers argue that firms must preserve value from non-financial resources such as people, intellectual property and nature, not just investors' money. So it calls for ecological data, such as greenhouse gas emissions, alongside financial figures. A 2009 meeting convened by the Prince of Wales set up the International Integrated Reporting Committee, or IIRC, to create a global framework. It was renamed a Council in November 2011. In 2021 the IIRC and the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board merged into the Value Reporting Foundation. By June 2022 the IFRS Foundation had folded that into its International Sustainability Standards Board.

nature-acct-101.title: SEEA Ecosystem Accounting: the UN standard for ecosystems
nature-acct-101.text: In March 2021, at its 52nd session, the UN Statistical Commission adopted SEEA Ecosystem Accounting as a standard. SEEA EA is a statistical framework that gives a consistent accounting approach for measuring ecosystems, within the wider SEEA family ({{ref:nature-found-013}}). Its accounts present three things: the extent of ecosystems, their condition, and the services they provide. These are kept in physical and money terms and tied to location. Its forerunner, the SEEA Experimental Ecosystem Accounts, built ecosystem accounts even though many of the stocks and flows are non-market assets, things never bought or sold. The next month, in April 2021, an AI-powered tool called the ARIES for SEEA Explorer was released for rapid, standardised natural capital accounting.

nature-acct-107.title: Depletion: writing off a resource as it is used up
nature-acct-107.text: Suppose a well holding 200,000 barrels of oil cost $100,000. If 10,000 barrels are extracted in the first year, the deduction is $5,000. That is cost depletion at work. Depletion means using up natural resources by mining, quarrying, drilling or felling. As an accounting and tax method, it records that gradual using up as an expense over time. Like depreciation, it lets owners recover costs as a resource's reserves shrink. For tax there are two types. Cost depletion spreads the resource's total cost over its estimated quantity, charging a share for each unit extracted; standing timber must use it. Percentage depletion multiplies a set percentage for each mineral by the property's gross income for the year. At national scale, country data are used to estimate the adjustments needed for the use and depletion of a nation's natural capital. Environmentalists use the figures to track resource use and hold governments to account. Economists use them to see how reliant countries or firms are on resources that do not renew.

nature-acct-109.title: Gross ecosystem product: GDP for nature's services
nature-acct-109.text: A 2020 study of Qinghai province in China found that nearly 80% of the benefits counted in its gross ecosystem product flowed to other provinces. Gross ecosystem product, or GEP, is the money value of the ecosystem services produced in an area over an accounting period, usually a year. It supplements GDP, which counts only market values and so misses the non-market value of ecosystem services. GEP sums material services such as fish, regulating services such as pollination and cultural services such as tourism, using market and non-market valuation ({{ref:nature-found-040}}). Zhiyun Ouyang and Chunquan Zhu first proposed it in 2013. The UN Statistical Commission adopted it within SEEA Ecosystem Accounting in 2021. China issued official GEP accounting guidelines in October 2022 and uses it in rural development, urban planning and {{ref:nature-mkt-136}}.

nature-acct-106.title: Wasting assets: things that lose value for good
nature-acct-106.text: A mine in use, a vehicle and an options contract share one trait: each loses value over time, and none gets it back. Accountants call such things wasting assets, assets that lose value irreversibly. Examples include vehicles, machinery, options contracts, which give a right to buy or sell at a set price before a deadline, and mines and quarries in use. Their decline may be handled for tax and other purposes through depreciation.

nature-acct-090.title: Environmental management accounting: data for decisions inside the firm
nature-acct-090.text: Corporate environmental accounting faces two ways. Environmental financial accounting reports outward, to investors, lenders and other outsiders. Environmental management accounting looks inward. It supports a firm's own decisions with physical and money data on its environmental use and costs. It gathers physical data on energy, water, materials and waste, plus money data on environment-related costs, earnings and savings.

nature-acct-091.title: Environmental reporting: telling stakeholders about impacts
nature-acct-091.text: A company's annual report, its sustainability report and its website may all carry the same kind of news: how the company affects the environment. Environmental reporting is the disclosure of an organisation's environmental impacts and performance. It may cover environmental risks and liabilities, energy and waste costs, emissions and pollution controls. It reaches stakeholders through annual reports, sustainability reports, integrated reports and websites.

nature-acct-095.title: Environmentally adjusted net domestic product: national product minus nature
nature-acct-095.text: Net domestic product is a standard figure in national accounts. The System of National Accounts defines it as net exports plus final consumption plus net investment. Its 'green' version, environmentally adjusted net domestic product, also called EDP or Green NDP, subtracts the using up of natural assets. Instead of the standard rules, it follows SEEA, which measures the depletion of scarce natural resources and the cost of environmental degradation and its prevention. EDP adds the net accumulation of produced and non-produced economic assets but deducts the net accumulation of non-produced natural assets.

nature-acct-093.title: The hidden price of producing and wasting food
nature-acct-093.text: The food the world wastes carries a hidden yearly bill: US$700 billion to natural capital and US$900 billion to social capital, by FAO estimates. Those figures come from applying full or true cost accounting to food, pricing the hidden environmental and social costs of food production and waste. The FAO's 2014 and 2015 studies looked at food wastage and at world food production's impact on natural capital. They put the environmental damage of world food production at US$2330 billion per year.

nature-acct-102.title: The residence principle: whose emissions are a ship's?
nature-acct-102.text: When a ship burns fuel far from home, which country's accounts should carry the emissions? Under SEEA's residence principle, the ship's home country. The rule counts all emissions caused by a country's economy, wherever they happen, rather than those released inside its borders. So emissions from trucks, ships or aircraft go to their home country even when released abroad. The emission counts kept under the UN climate convention ({{ref:nature-clim-053}}) use geographic borders instead, so the two approaches differ mainly for transport. Those counts also treat transport as its own sector, hiding the shares of households and industries.

nature-acct-104.title: The trillions hidden in the world's food bill
nature-acct-104.text: Feeding the world costs far more than their prices show. Estimates of their hidden environmental, health and social costs, the ones market prices leave out, run to trillions of dollars. FOLU put them at USD 12 trillion in 2019. Hendricks and colleagues, in 2023, estimated USD 19 trillion, within a range of USD 7.2 to 51.8 trillion. The FAO's 2023 State of Food and Agriculture, assessing 154 countries one by one, arrived at USD 12.7 trillion. The largest share is not environmental. FAO later found that health costs from unhealthy diets made up 70 percent of all agrifood hidden costs in 2020.

nature-acct-098.title: Repetto's green accounts for Indonesia
nature-acct-098.text: In 1990 a study by {{ref:nature-hist-032}} redid Indonesia's national accounts with nature included. It subtracted the net depreciation of petroleum, timber and soils from GDP to estimate an environmentally adjusted net domestic product. Conventional accounts, it found, overstated net income and its growth. Environmental costs equalled 4.9% of Indonesia's NDP in 1990, mainly from changes in how land was used ({{ref:nature-res-108}}) and from oil extraction.

nature-acct-097.title: WAVES: helping countries put nature in their accounts
nature-acct-097.text: In October 2010 the World Bank launched a global partnership called Wealth Accounting and Valuation of Ecosystem Services, or WAVES. The launch came at the COP-10 meeting of the UN biodiversity treaty ({{ref:nature-gov-015}}) in Japan. It helps countries put the value of natural capital into their national accounts. Its projects in countries such as Botswana, Colombia and Madagascar built the capacity to apply SEEA. The World Bank now runs a successor, the Global Program for Sustainability.

nature-acct-108.title: Environmental profit and loss: Puma's price tag on nature
nature-acct-108.text: Puma produced the first environmental profit and loss account, on 2010 data. It valued greenhouse gases, water use, other air pollution, land conversion and waste. Such an account is a company's money valuation of its environmental impacts across its own operations and its supply chain, from raw materials to the factory gate. It internalises externalities, bringing outside costs onto the books, by counting the ecosystem services a business depends on as well as the damage it causes. Its main purpose is to show managers and stakeholders how large the impacts are and where in the supply chain they occur. The method built on models of how industries buy from one another ({{ref:nature-acct-080}}) and on valuation work in environmental economics, such as the TEEB study. Philips's 2017 annual report used it to put that year's environmental impact at Euro 7.2 billion. Preparing one can be expensive. It is seen as a first step toward prices that reflect the use of environmental goods and services.

nature-acct-112.title: Material flow indicators: summing up an economy's appetite
nature-acct-112.text: Material flow accounts yield a set of standard indicators that summarise an economy's material use. Direct material input is domestic extraction plus imports; domestic material consumption subtracts exports from that. The physical trade balance is imports minus exports, the reverse of the money trade balance, because goods and money flow in opposite directions. Total material requirement adds hidden flows, materials moved but not used, such as mining overburden, the rock cleared to reach ore. Raw material consumption counts the raw materials embodied in traded goods, usually via {{ref:nature-acct-071}}.

nature-acct-113.title: SEEA-Water: putting water into the national accounts
nature-acct-113.text: SEEA-Water is the UN's framework for organising physical and economic information about water, using the same concepts and classifications as the System of National Accounts. That match lets hydrological and water-use data be combined with economic data. The framework sorts water stocks and flows into two systems: inland water, covering the natural water cycle, and the economy, covering water-using industries and households. The UN Statistical Commission adopted it as an interim statistical standard in 2007. More than fifty countries are implementing or planning water accounts.

nature-acct-115.title: El Serafy's method for pricing resource depletion
nature-acct-115.text: Salah El Serafy devised a method for valuing the depletion cost of natural resources, one of several ways to estimate {{ref:nature-res-239}} in national accounts. The alternatives compared with it are net price, sustainable price, transaction value and replacement cost. El Serafy co-edited a report on economic accounting for lasting development from UNEP-World Bank workshops held after 1983. He disagreed with Anne Harrison. She wanted adjustments made inside the existing System of National Accounts, while he proposed redefining intermediate and final demand. Experts still split along the same line, as the dispute over green GDP shows ({{ref:nature-acct-010}}).

openers.national-and-corporate-natural-capital-a: A firm's books record what it owns or controls, its {{ref:nature-acct-105}}, yet many effects of its activity on nature stay hidden from them. This chapter follows the efforts to change that. {{ref:nature-acct-089}} measures and reports environmental impacts, in money and in physical units, for firms and for whole nations. {{ref:nature-acct-096}} adds up the stocks and flows of natural resources and services in a region, and the UN's {{ref:nature-acct-101}} gives ecosystem accounts a consistent method. Companies, meanwhile, have tried {{ref:nature-acct-114}}, {{ref:nature-acct-103}} and {{ref:nature-acct-110}}, each a way of setting nature's costs beside the profits.

reviews.national-and-corporate-natural-capital-a: Every account in this chapter tries to move nature onto the books. Firms do it inward, through environmental management accounting, and outward, through sustainability accounting, integrated reports and environmental profit and loss accounts like Puma's. Nations do it through natural capital accounting, which SEEA Ecosystem Accounting and SEEA-Water standardise, and through depletion adjustments like Repetto's for Indonesia, where conventional accounts overstated income. The hidden costs uncovered can be enormous: the FAO put those of the world's agrifood systems at USD 12.7 trillion. Yet the methods remain contested, from the arbitrariness of valuing externalities to whether the triple bottom line works in practice.
